A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same T3CEN research, with matching authors, core construction, and retained experiments. All 24 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v3, including figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-D, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original equivariance-error measurements and classification experiments on synthetic shapes, natural images, small NORB, and Camelyon17, plus MNIST analyses in the appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds augmentation comparisons, tomato-ripeness and MNIST failure-condition experiments, redundancy measurements, and computational benchmarks.

M1.justification: The double-cover lifting, discretized HSL groups, group convolutions, and classification pooling are retained. RGB and scale extensions already appeared in v1; their relocation to v3's Discussion does not introduce a method component.

E1.justification: v3 adds KUTomaData tomato-ripeness classification, where absolute color predicts the label, and controlled MNIST scenarios with identical or mildly shifted train-test hue distributions. These extend evaluation to important task conditions beyond v1's disjoint-hue MNIST experiment and nuisance-color robustness emphasis. Existing dataset coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 5, v3 Table 6 adds ResNet-AugMix and ResNet-DeepAug to both saturation and luminance comparisons, and Planckian jitter, labeled ResNet-Plackian, to saturation comparisons. This substantially expands evaluated augmentation alternatives across six datasets. The existing ResNet-aug row is renamed ResNet-Jitter, rather than constituting another added comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix D.6 changes the reported Camelyon17 train/validation/test hospitals from 1,2,3/4/5 to 0,3,4/2/1; unchanged result values do not establish reruns. New protocols include 200-epoch KUTomaData training, 1,000-iteration MNIST comparisons at 0, 5, 10, and 15 degrees of shift, and ResNet18 resource measurements after 100 warm-up iterations. Most retained training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.5 directly tests failure when color identifies the class and when distribution shift is absent or small. Appendix C.4 measures how frequently redundant lifting occurs across six datasets, whereas v1 only analyzed its mathematical occurrence. Appendix D.8 adds measured computational scaling. Existing cardinality, coverage, and equivariance-error analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D retains the stated three-seed and five-seed protocols and the existing parenthesized variability reporting. Added augmentation rows follow that practice; the new failure-condition tables provide point results without introducing explicit seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance procedures. Changed parenthesized values are result changes.

E6.justification: New results include KUTomaData errors of 31.75 for T3CEN-H4 versus 19.13 for ResNet18, MNIST accuracy across shift magnitudes, augmentation comparisons, redundancy percentages, and resource measurements. Retained rows also change: saturation-shifted CIFAR-100 T3CEN-S4 error changes from 44.27 (1.70) to 41.35 (1.27), its CIFAR-10 entry from 11.59 (1.33) to 11.59 (1.39), and luminance-shifted Caltech-101 ResNet-aug/Jitter error from 30.82 to 57.03. The PDFs do not explain these revisions.

T1.justification: The existing equations, group constructions, and Appendix B proofs are retained. New Appendix C.4 refines the redundancy definition by explicitly distinguishing fully redundant inputs at 0.5 from partially redundant inputs at 0.25 or 0.75. No new equivariance proof or revised derivation accompanies this limited addition.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same headline contributions: perfect HSL equivariance through double-cover lifting, improved robustness and predictive performance, and applicability to RGB and scale transformations. The added experiments do not replace these core contribution statements.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's computational-cost, large-cardinality, and lifting-degeneracy discussions, v3 explains two substantive applicability boundaries. Invariant classification pooling can suppress label-relevant color, while reduced filter width can hurt performance without sufficient distribution shift. Section 5.5 connects these mechanisms to the new experiments and explicitly identifies the conditions favoring T3CEN.

D1.justification: v3 adds measured memory and training throughput, identifying nvidia-smi and tqdm and specifying that the first 100 iterations are discarded before averaging the next 100. It also supplies training budgets for the new failure-condition experiments. Existing hardware descriptions and the main hyperparameter table remain essentially unchanged; the new experiments are not documented comprehensively.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for KUTomaData, Planckian jitter, Özmen's Deepaugment, and tqdm. The related-work discussion and positioning against earlier color-equivariant methods remain substantially unchanged. Publication updates for existing references, including Adam and Polar Transformer Networks, are not new cited works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains close to v1. Local edits replace degenerate-lifting terminology with redundant representations, move RGB and scale applications into a separate Discussion, and add impact and acknowledgement sections. Section 4 is retitled Background, duplicating Section 3's heading. These are limited editorial and structural changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, several comparison tables are transposed, and Figure 1 is redrawn as lifting and cyclic-permutation diagrams. RGB and scale panels are separated, while dataset-example figures are merged. New failure-condition, redundancy, and computation tables and tomato examples substantially extend the displays.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny and practical applicability guidance: it directly demonstrates important failure conditions, broadens augmentation comparisons, and replaces a generic computational-cost warning with measurements. These address important gaps in v1's evaluation. The gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including sparse details for new experiments and the unexplained Camelyon17 split revision. The broad superiority wording also needs qualification: v3 Table 6 reports saturation-shifted Caltech-101 error of 35.53 for AugMix versus 40.02 for the best listed T3CEN variant.
